## Analyzing Condition 2 (Coprime Partition)

**Claim:** $n$ must be squarefree.

*Proof.* Let $n = p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}$. A divisor $d$ using *all* primes of $n$ (i.e., every $p_i \mid d$) is coprime only to $1$, since any other divisor $e>1$ shares some prime with $d$. The number of such divisors is $\prod a_i$. If any $a_i \ge 2$, this product is $\ge 2$, giving at least 2 divisors that can only pair with $1$—impossible since $1$ pairs with just one. So all $a_i = 1$, meaning $n$ is squarefree. $\square$

For squarefree $n$, the pairing $\{d, n/d\}$ always gives coprime pairs (each prime goes entirely to one side).

**Uniqueness:** I claim the complement matching $\{d, n/d\}$ is the *only* coprime partition. The divisor $n$ (all primes) is coprime only to $1$, forcing $\{1,n\}$. Then $n/p_i$ (all primes except $p_i$) is coprime only to divisors of $p_i$, namely $1$ and $p_i$
